title: Problem Statement and Background
content: Erdős Problem #1139 concerns the sequence of integers with at most 2 prime factors counted with multiplicity (the P₂ numbers or almost-primes). This includes all primes (Ω = 1) and all semiprimes p·q (Ω = 2), forming a much denser sequence than the primes alone. The question asks whether gaps in this sequence still grow faster than log k, which would be surprising given the abundance of almost-primes. The problem dates to Erdős's investigations into the distribution of integers classified by their number of prime factors.
mathContext: The sequence $u_1 < u_2 < \cdots$ consists of all $n$ with $\Omega(n) \leq 2$, where $\Omega(n) = \sum_{p^a \| n} a$ counts prime factors with multiplicity. The conjecture asks: $\limsup_{k \to \infty} \frac{u_{k+1} - u_k}{\log k} = \infty$.

title: Big Omega Function via Factorization
content: Defines Ω(n) as the sum of exponents in the prime factorization of n, using Mathlib's Finsupp-valued factorization. For n = p₁^a₁ · p₂^a₂ · ⋯ · pₖ^aₖ, we get Ω(n) = a₁ + a₂ + ⋯ + aₖ. This is noncomputable because Mathlib's factorization relies on classical decidability of primality.
mathContext: $\Omega(n) = \sum_{p \mid n} v_p(n)$, where $v_p(n)$ is the $p$-adic valuation. Examples: $\Omega(12) = \Omega(2^2 \cdot 3) = 3$, $\Omega(p) = 1$ for primes.

title: Almost-Prime Predicate and Decidable Check
content: IsAlmostPrime n holds when n ≥ 2 and Ω(n) ≤ 2. The n ≥ 2 condition excludes 0 and 1, which are conventionally not considered almost-prime. The computable checkAlmostPrime uses primeFactorsList (the list of prime factors with repetition) rather than the noncomputable factorization, enabling native_decide proofs for small cases.
mathContext: $n$ is a $P_2$-number (almost-prime) iff $n \geq 2$ and $\Omega(n) \leq 2$. The $P_k$-numbers generalize this to $\Omega(n) \leq k$.

title: Every Prime is Almost-Prime
content: The proof that every prime p satisfies IsAlmostPrime p proceeds by showing: (1) p ≥ 2 from Nat.Prime.two_le, and (2) Ω(p) = 1 ≤ 2 by rewriting with Nat.Prime.factorization, which gives the factorization of a prime as a single entry {p ↦ 1}, so the sum is 1. The simp with Finsupp.sum_single_index completes the computation.
mathContext: For prime $p$: $\Omega(p) = v_p(p) = 1 \leq 2$, so every prime is automatically a $P_2$-number.

title: Small Cases: Boundary Between Almost-Primes and Non-Almost-Primes
content: These theorems establish the boundary of the almost-prime predicate on small numbers. Notably, 4 = 2² has Ω(4) = 2 (almost-prime) while 8 = 2³ has Ω(8) = 3 (not almost-prime). The proof for 4 uses native_decide to computationally verify the factorization, while 8's proof proceeds by contradiction: assuming Ω(8) ≤ 2 and using native_decide to refute it. These small cases illustrate that the almost-prime sequence is 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 9, 10, 11, 13, 14, 15, ... with 8, 16, 24, ... excluded.
mathContext: $\Omega(4) = \Omega(2^2) = 2 \leq 2$ (almost-prime), but $\Omega(8) = \Omega(2^3) = 3 > 2$ (not almost-prime). The first non-almost-prime after 1 is 8.

title: Almost-Prime Enumeration and Gaps
content: Defines almostPrimesUpTo N as the finite set of almost-primes in {0, ..., N}, using the decidable checkAlmostPrime filter. The gap function almostPrimeGap k gives the difference u_{k+1} - u_k between consecutive almost-primes; it is left as sorry because defining the k-th element of a filtered sequence requires well-founded recursion on the enumeration, which is nontrivial to formalize.
mathContext: $\pi_2(N) = |\{n \leq N : \Omega(n) \leq 2\}|$ is the almost-prime counting function. The gap sequence is $g_k = u_{k+1} - u_k$.

title: Structural Results: Primes and Semiprimes
content: Two structural results: (1) primes_subset_almostPrimes is a direct corollary of prime_isAlmostPrime. (2) semiprime_isAlmostPrime shows that every product of two primes p·q is almost-prime: p·q ≥ 4 (from p,q ≥ 2) and Ω(p·q) = Ω(p) + Ω(q) = 2 (the sorry remains because proving the additivity Ω(p·q) = Ω(p) + Ω(q) for coprime arguments requires careful manipulation of Mathlib's factorization API for products).
mathContext: For primes $p, q$: $\Omega(pq) = \Omega(p) + \Omega(q) = 1 + 1 = 2$, using the complete additivity of $\Omega$ on coprime arguments. The bound $pq \geq 2 \cdot 2 = 4$ is tight when $p = q = 2$.

title: Primes Contained in Almost-Primes
content: Proves that the set of primes up to N is a subset of almostPrimesUpTo N. The proof unfolds almostPrimesUpTo and checkAlmostPrime, then uses Nat.primeFactorsList_prime to show that a prime p has primeFactorsList = [p], so the length is 1 ≤ 2. This containment is the key ingredient for showing π₂(N) ≥ π(N) ~ N/log N, establishing that almost-primes are at least as dense as primes.
mathContext: $\{p \leq N : p \text{ prime}\} \subseteq \{n \leq N : \Omega(n) \leq 2\}$, hence $\pi_2(N) \geq \pi(N) \sim N/\log N$ by the Prime Number Theorem.

title: The Main Conjecture: Unbounded Normalized Gaps
content: The axiom erdos_1139 formalizes the conjecture as: for every constant C > 0 and every starting index K, there exists k ≥ K with gap(k) > C·log(k). This is the ε-δ formulation of lim sup = ∞. The conjecture asserts that despite almost-primes being much denser than primes (by a factor of log log N), their gaps can still be arbitrarily large relative to log k. This would contrast with the situation for primes, where the prime number theorem implies average gap ~ log p_k.
mathContext: $\limsup_{k \to \infty} \frac{u_{k+1} - u_k}{\log k} = \infty$ means: $\forall C > 0,\; \forall K \in \mathbb{N},\; \exists k \geq K,\; u_{k+1} - u_k > C \log k$.

title: Cube Gap Obstruction: Divisibility by 8
content: This theorem shows that if m is divisible by 8 and lies between consecutive cubes n³ and (n+1)³, then m is not almost-prime. Since 8 = 2³ means Ω(8k) ≥ 3, any multiple of 8 has too many prime factors. This provides a structural explanation for why gaps in the almost-prime sequence can be large: in intervals where multiples of 8 dominate (and other highly composite numbers cluster), the almost-prime sequence must skip over them, creating gaps.
mathContext: If $8 \mid m$, then $\Omega(m) \geq \Omega(8) = 3 > 2$, so $m$ is not a $P_2$-number. Between $n^3$ and $(n+1)^3$, multiples of 8 appear with spacing 8, creating regions where almost-primes are sparse.

title: Hardy-Ramanujan Asymptotic for Almost-Prime Density
content: This axiom encodes the Landau-Ramanujan theorem specialized to k ≤ 2: the number of almost-primes up to X satisfies π₂(X) ~ c·X·log(log X)/log X for a positive constant c. The extra log log X factor compared to the Prime Number Theorem (π(X) ~ X/log X) arises because semiprimes p·q contribute an additional logarithmic factor from summing 1/p over primes p. This density result is central to the problem: despite almost-primes being denser than primes, Erdős conjectured their gaps still grow faster than log k.
mathContext: By the Landau-Ramanujan theorem, $\pi_2(X) \sim c \cdot \frac{X \log \log X}{\log X}$ as $X \to \infty$. The average gap between consecutive $P_2$-numbers near $X$ is thus $\sim \frac{\log X}{c \log \log X}$, which grows slower than $\log X$ but still tends to infinity.
